        <header class="article-header">
            <div class="article-category"><i class="fas fa-dragon"></i> Ransomware</div>
            <h1>DragonForce: The New Ransomware Cartel Built on LockBit and Conti DNA</h1>
            <p class="article-excerpt">From pro-Palestinian hacktivists to profit-driven ransomware cartel.
                DragonForce has emerged as a formidable threat by combining leaked code from LockBit 3.0 and Conti
                into a powerful RaaS platform that's already claimed high-profile victims.</p>
            <div class="article-meta">
                <span><i class="far fa-calendar-alt"></i> Threat Active: 2023 - Present</span>
                <span><i class="fas fa-clock"></i> Published: Jan 20, 2026</span>
                <span><i class="fas fa-book-open"></i> 18 min read</span>
                <span><i class="fas fa-user"></i> By Harish G</span>
            </div>
        </header>

        <img src="/images/articles/dragonforce-ransomware-cartel-2026.png"
            alt="DragonForce Ransomware Cartel Analysis" class="featured-image" loading="lazy">

        <div class="threat-actor-box">
            <span class="actor-name"><i class="fas fa-dragon"></i> DragonForce</span>
            <span class="label">Ransomware Cartel | LockBit 3.0 + Conti DNA | RaaS Platform</span>
        </div>

        <div class="critical-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-skull-crossbones"></i> ACTIVE THREAT:</strong> DragonForce has evolved from a
            hacktivist collective into one of the most aggressive ransomware cartels of 2026. By leveraging leaked
            source code from LockBit 3.0 and Conti, they've built a sophisticated RaaS operation that's absorbing
            rival groups and targeting high-value organizations worldwide.
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-history"></i> The Evolution: From Hacktivists to Criminal Enterprise</h2>

        <p>DragonForce didn't start as a ransomware operation. The group emerged in 2023 as a pro-Palestinian
            hacktivist collective, conducting DDoS attacks and website defacements against Israeli targets. But
            somewhere along the way, the operators realized there was more money in extortion than ideology.</p>

        <p>By late 2023, DragonForce had pivoted to ransomware, and by March 2025, they formally rebranded as a
            "cartel" — launching an affiliate program that invites other cybercriminals to use their platform in
            exchange for a cut of the profits.</p>

        <div class="timeline">
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">2023</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">DragonForce emerges as a pro-Palestinian hacktivist group conducting
                    DDoS attacks and defacements.</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">Late 2023</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Pivot to ransomware operations begins. Group starts using modified
                    ransomware tools.</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">2024</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Integration of LockBit 3.0 leaked source code. Ransomware capabilities
                    significantly enhanced.</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">March 2025</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Formal rebrand as a "cartel." Launch of affiliate program and RaaS
                    platform "Ransombay."</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">May 2025</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">High-profile attacks on UK retailers: Marks & Spencer, Co-op, Harrods
                    targeted.</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">August 2025</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Introduction of "data analysis service" to increase pressure on
                    victims.</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">January 2026</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Continued expansion. Active absorption of rival ransomware operations
                    into the cartel.</span>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-code"></i> The DNA: LockBit 3.0 + Conti Source Code</h2>

        <p>What makes DragonForce particularly dangerous is their ransomware's genetic makeup. Rather than building
            from scratch, the group has incorporated leaked source code from two of history's most successful
            ransomware operations:</p>

        <h3>LockBit 3.0 (LockBit Black)</h3>

        <p>When a disgruntled LockBit developer leaked the LockBit 3.0 source code in September 2022, it became a
            gift that keeps giving to the cybercriminal ecosystem. DragonForce has heavily leveraged this code,
            which included:</p>

        <ul>
            <li><strong>Advanced encryption routines:</strong> Fast, efficient file encryption that minimizes
                detection time</li>
            <li><strong>Anti-analysis features:</strong> Techniques to evade security researchers and sandboxes</li>
            <li><strong>Self-propagation capabilities:</strong> Ability to spread laterally through networks</li>
            <li><strong>Credential harvesting:</strong> Built-in tools to extract passwords and tokens</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Conti Source Code</h3>

        <p>After the Conti group imploded following their attack on Costa Rica in 2022, their source code also found
            its way into the wild. DragonForce has incorporated Conti's:</p>

        <ul>
            <li><strong>Network reconnaissance modules:</strong> Sophisticated scanning for valuable targets</li>
            <li><strong>Active Directory exploitation:</strong> Tools for domain compromise</li>
            <li><strong>Data exfiltration pipelines:</strong> Efficient extraction of sensitive files</li>
            <li><strong>Negotiation playbooks:</strong> Proven tactics for extracting payments</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Why This Matters:</strong> By combining code from two highly
            successful operations, DragonForce has essentially created a "greatest hits" ransomware that
            incorporates years of criminal R&D without the original development costs.
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-users"></i> The Cartel Model: RaaS 2.0</h2>

        <p>DragonForce's cartel model represents an evolution in Ransomware-as-a-Service. Their platform, called
            "Ransombay," offers affiliates a comprehensive toolkit:</p>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Feature</th>
                    <th>Description</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Ransomware Builder</strong></td>
                    <td>Customizable payloads with LockBit/Conti DNA</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Leak Site Hosting</strong></td>
                    <td>Centralized infrastructure for victim shaming</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Negotiation Portal</strong></td>
                    <td>Professional chat interface for ransom discussions</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Data Analysis Service</strong></td>
                    <td>Team reviews stolen data to identify leverage points</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Payment Processing</strong></td>
                    <td>Cryptocurrency laundering and distribution</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Technical Support</strong></td>
                    <td>24/7 assistance for affiliates</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>Revenue Sharing</h3>

        <p>Like other RaaS operations, DragonForce takes a percentage of each ransom payment. Reports suggest they
            operate on a 70/30 or 80/20 split favoring affiliates, which makes them competitive in the crowded
            ransomware market.</p>

        <h3>Absorbing the Competition</h3>

        <p>What truly distinguishes DragonForce's cartel approach is their strategy of absorbing rival operations.
            Rather than competing with smaller ransomware groups, they're offering to bring them under the
            DragonForce umbrella — providing better infrastructure, more victims, and shared resources. This
            consolidation strategy mirrors legitimate business practices and suggests sophisticated leadership.</p>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-building"></i> Notable Victims: UK Retail Under Siege</h2>

        <p>DragonForce made international headlines in 2025 when they launched a coordinated campaign against major
            UK retailers:</p>

        <div class="victim-card">
            <h4><i class="fas fa-store"></i> Marks & Spencer</h4>
            <p>The iconic British retailer was hit in early 2025, with DragonForce claiming to have exfiltrated
                customer data and internal documents. The attack disrupted operations and forced temporary system
                shutdowns.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="victim-card">
            <h4><i class="fas fa-shopping-cart"></i> The Co-operative Group (Co-op)</h4>
            <p>The UK's fifth-largest food retailer suffered a significant breach. DragonForce threatened to release
                employee data, supplier contracts, and financial information.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="victim-card">
            <h4><i class="fas fa-gem"></i> Harrods</h4>
            <p>The luxury department store was targeted in the same campaign, demonstrating DragonForce's confidence
                in taking on high-profile, well-resourced targets.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="stat-grid">
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value orange">3</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Major UK Retailers Hit</span>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value">2025</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Cartel Launch Year</span>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value cyan">4x</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Extortion Methods</span>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value orange">Active</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Current Status</span>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-bomb"></i> Attack Methodology: Multi-Extortion Tactics</h2>

        <p>DragonForce employs a four-pronged extortion strategy that maximizes pressure on victims:</p>

        <div class="attack-chain">
            <span class="attack-chain-step">1. Encrypt Files</span>
            <span class="attack-chain-arrow"><i class="fas fa-arrow-right"></i></span>
            <span class="attack-chain-step">2. Steal Data</span>
            <span class="attack-chain-arrow"><i class="fas fa-arrow-right"></i></span>
            <span class="attack-chain-step">3. Threaten Leak</span>
            <span class="attack-chain-arrow"><i class="fas fa-arrow-right"></i></span>
            <span class="attack-chain-step">4. Contact Victims</span>
        </div>

        <h3>1. File Encryption</h3>
        <p>Traditional ransomware encryption renders files unusable until a decryption key is purchased.
            DragonForce's encryption is fast and thorough, prioritizing high-value file types.</p>

        <h3>2. Data Exfiltration</h3>
        <p>Before encryption, DragonForce systematically identifies and extracts sensitive data — financial records,
            customer databases, employee information, intellectual property, and trade secrets.</p>

        <h3>3. Public Leaks</h3>
        <p>Stolen data is threatened for release on their leak site. They often release "samples" to prove they have
            the data and demonstrate the consequences of non-payment.</p>

        <h3>4. Direct Communication</h3>
        <p>DragonForce doesn't just threaten — they act. Affiliates have been known to directly contact employees,
            partners, and even customers to amplify pressure on victim organizations.</p>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Data Analysis Service:</strong> In August 2025,
            DragonForce introduced a "data analysis service" where their team reviews stolen data to identify
            specific leverage points — executive communications, legal issues, regulatory violations — that can be
            used to increase ransom demands. This professionalized approach to extortion represents a concerning
            escalation.
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-globe"></i> The Broader Ransomware Landscape in 2026</h2>

        <p>DragonForce's rise occurs against a evolving ransomware backdrop. Key trends include:</p>

        <h3>LockBit's Resurrection</h3>
        <p>Despite Operation Cronos disrupting LockBit in early 2024, the group announced a comeback in September
            2025 with "LockBit 5.0" and is actively recruiting new affiliates. They remain a major threat,
            particularly to healthcare organizations.</p>

        <h3>Code Sharing Economy</h3>
        <p>The leaking of LockBit and Conti source code has democratized ransomware development. Groups like
            DragonForce can build sophisticated operations without starting from zero.</p>

        <h3>Geographic Expansion</h3>
        <p>For the first time in 2026, analysts predict that new ransomware actors operating outside Russia will
            outnumber those within it. This global expansion makes attribution and law enforcement more challenging.
        </p>

        <h3>AI Integration</h3>
        <p>Ransomware groups are beginning to integrate AI capabilities into their operations — from automated
            reconnaissance to AI-powered social engineering. This trend is expected to accelerate throughout 2026.
        </p>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> Defense Recommendations</h2>

        <p>Protecting against DragonForce and similar cartels requires a multi-layered approach:</p>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Immediate Actions:</strong>
            <ul>
                <li><strong>Patch aggressively:</strong> DragonForce exploits known vulnerabilities. Prioritize CISA
                    KEV catalog items.</li>
                <li><strong>Implement MFA everywhere:</strong> Credential theft is a primary access vector.</li>
                <li><strong>Segment networks:</strong> Limit lateral movement once access is gained.</li>
                <li><strong>Monitor for data exfiltration:</strong> Large outbound transfers are a red flag.</li>
                <li><strong>Maintain offline backups:</strong> 3-2-1 backup strategy with tested restoration.</li>
                <li><strong>Train employees:</strong> Phishing remains a common initial access vector.</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <h3>Detection Indicators</h3>

        <p>Organizations should monitor for:</p>

        <ul>
            <li>Unusual process execution patterns consistent with LockBit/Conti TTPs</li>
            <li>Attempts to disable security tools or backup solutions</li>
            <li>Large-scale file enumeration across network shares</li>
            <li>Connections to known DragonForce infrastructure (check threat feeds)</li>
            <li>Use of legitimate tools (PsExec, Cobalt Strike) for lateral movement</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Incident Response Preparation</h3>

        <p>Given DragonForce's multi-extortion model, organizations should prepare for scenarios where:</p>

        <ul>
            <li>Data has been stolen regardless of whether encryption occurred</li>
            <li>Attackers may contact employees, partners, or customers directly</li>
            <li>Regulatory notification may be required even without ransom payment</li>
            <li>Reputation management becomes as important as technical recovery</li>
        </ul>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-key"></i> Key Takeaways</h2>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-list"></i> Summary:</strong>
            <ol>
                <li><strong>DragonForce has evolved</strong> from hacktivists to one of the most aggressive
                    ransomware cartels of 2026</li>
                <li><strong>Their ransomware combines</strong> leaked LockBit 3.0 and Conti source code for maximum
                    effectiveness</li>
                <li><strong>The cartel model</strong> includes a RaaS platform, affiliate program, and absorption of
                    rival groups</li>
                <li><strong>Multi-extortion tactics</strong> include encryption, data theft, leak threats, and
                    direct victim contact</li>
                <li><strong>High-profile UK retailers</strong> Marks & Spencer, Co-op, and Harrods have been
                    targeted</li>
                <li><strong>Defense requires</strong> aggressive patching, network segmentation, and preparation for
                    data theft scenarios</li>
            </ol>
        </div>
